I have 13.1 mu total, so I will not spread myself too thin. On about 8.1 mu I will keep the wheat-maize rotation, because that is the steady income in our area and I know this system well. The other 5 mu I will keep in cotton. I only studied to middle school, so I do listen when people talk about rates, but in the end I still farm by what I have seen on my own land and what the neighbors do. Wheat and maize together are safer for me than putting everything into cotton, because if one side has a bad year, at least I still have the other. Some people in my family work off-farm, so labor is tight at busy times, and I have to keep the plan practical and not too expensive. I have a well, so I can irrigate when the crop really needs it, but pumping costs money, so I will not water too freely.

For wheat, I will use the same 8.1 mu as usual and sow in early October with a common improved local variety. I usually put base fertilizer before sowing, then topdress once around jointing. I do not want the wheat to go hungry, because if the leaves turn yellow in spring the yield falls quickly, and making that back is hard. Still, fertilizer is expensive, so I will keep it around a medium level, not the highest. I will water about three times if the season is normal: once before winter if the soil is dry, once at jointing, and once around grain filling if needed. After wheat harvest in June, I will turn that same land quickly into summer maize. The turnaround is short, so I will use simple rotary tillage or even reduced tillage if the custom machine is available, just to save time. For maize I will use hybrid seed, put most fertilizer early, and give one topdress around the big bell stage if the crop looks strong enough to justify it. Irrigation for maize depends on rain; if summer rain is normal I may only irrigate once or not at all, but with the well I can give one or two waterings if it turns dry. Cotton is more work, but I will keep 5 mu because it still spreads risk. I will not push cotton too hard with fertilizer because it ties up money for a long time and needs more picking labor. I will manage it steadily, use plastic mulch if I can get it at a fair price, irrigate a couple of times, and spray only when I really see pressure.
